papers.title_in_file: Observation of Distinct Phase Transitions in a Nonlinear Optical Ising Machine
papers.version_note: arXiv:2209.06269v2 [physics.optics], 16 Sep 2022 (dated September 19, 2022 in the header). The text is the paper the record names.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental and numerical study of ferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic phase transitions in an SLM and second-harmonic-generation optical Ising machine with two-body and four-body spin interactions, with a mean-field explanation.

assertions.value: The authors report a mode-locked pump laser of wavelength 1550.9nm and average power 70mW, with a pump beam full width half maximum of 3.8mm incident on the SLM.
quotes: We use a mode-locked laser of wavelength λ ∼ 1550.9nm with an average power of 70mW as the pump light.
The full width half maximum of the pump beam is wp = 3.8mm which is incident on the SLM
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in the Experimental setup section.

assertions.value: The authors report an SLM (Santec SLM-100) with 1440×1050 pixels and pixel length a = 10µm. The region of interest is a square lattice of N = 20 × 20 giant spins, each spin consisting of 20×20 pixels of the same phase.
quotes: (Santec SLM-100, 1440×1050 pixels, pixel length a = 10µm)
a square lattice of N = 20 × 20 giant spins with each spin consisting of 20×20 pixels of the same phase
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup stated in the Experimental setup section.
assertions.reader_inference: N = 20 × 20 is 400 spins; the mean-field formulas use N for the spin count, so N = 400 there (consistent with the paper's gamma_c of about 55: J/(6 N^2 K) with J 0.19, K 3.6e-9 gives 55 only for N = 400).

assertions.value: The authors report a lens of focal length F = 200mm focusing the modulated beam into a temperature-stabilized periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) crystal (5mol.% MgO-doped PPLN, length 1cm from HC Photonics), which generates a second harmonic (SH) light at about 775.5nm.
quotes: A lens with focal length F = 200mm is used to focus the modulated beam into a temperature-stabilized periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) crystal
Λ=19.36µm (5mol.% MgO-doped PPLN, length 1cm from HC Photonics). It generates a SH light at λh ∼ 775.5nm
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup stated in the Experimental setup section.

assertions.value: The authors report that power-meter measurements go to a computer MATLAB interface that completes the feedback loop by updating the SLM, and that each spin flip is accepted or rejected with a Boltzmann probability P = exp(−∆U/T), where ∆U = Enew −Eold is the change in energy of a target Hamiltonian and T is the effective temperature.
quotes: The measurements are sent to the computer MATLAB interface, which completes the feedback loop by updating the SLM [36].
The spin ﬂipping during each iteration is accepted or rejected according to a Boltzmann probability function P = exp(−∆U/T ), where ∆U = Enew −Eold is the change in energy

σi = ±1 is the phase of the pump light

assertions.value: The authors define the Ising Hamiltonian of the machine as the superposition of the pump and SH light intensities; the pump intensity is multiplied by −1 so that a ferromagnetic phase is favored at T = 0, and gamma is a tunable parameter. The two terms correspond to a two-body and a four-body spin interaction.
quotes: The Hamiltonian of our Ising spin model is deﬁned as
the superposition of the pump and SH light intensities,
where we have multiplied −1 for pump light intensity (so that a ferromagnetic phase is favored at T = 0) and γ is a tunable parameter.
It is clear that the two terms correspond to a two-body and a four-body spin interaction
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition given by the paper in Eq. (4) and the text after it.

assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the equation that defines Pi and Qij; the rank statement itself is quoted but the derivation is not in the text. Rank N here is as printed; the paper does not say whether N is the spin count 400.

assertions.value: The authors state that such low-rank two-body and four-body spin interactions may impose some limitations to the SLM-based optical Ising machine for solving complex optimization problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that the low-rank limitation can be circumvented, for example by adding a scattering medium in front of the detector (proposed in recent work), by changing the relative locations of the Fourier lenses to induce non-negligible diffraction inside the crystal, or by raising the pump power into the pump-depletion regime; in either of the last two cases Jij and Kijsr become full rank matrices. No experiment of these options is reported in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that, at a fixed effective temperature, the Ising energy decreases to its lowest value after some Monte-Carlo iterations and the magnetization increases from zero (the start is a random spin configuration) to a finite value that depends on the four-body coefficient.
quotes: the Ising energy decreases to its lowest value after some
Monte-Carlo iterations and the corresponding magnetization increases from zero (as we start with an initial random spin conﬁguration) to a ﬁnite value that depends on the four-body coeﬃcient.
assertions.reader_inference: The Fig. 2 caption says gamma = 1 and 500 for panels (a,b).

assertions.value: The authors report an experimental observation of two distinct ferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic transitions as the effective temperature increases: the magnetization changes to zero continuously for gamma = 0, 100, and drops to zero abruptly for gamma = 500, which they identify as second-order and first-order phase transitions respectively. Tuning is by the ratio of the light intensities at the fundamental and second-harmonic frequencies.
quotes: By tuning the ratio of the light intensities at the fundamental and secondharmonic frequencies
the magnetization changes to zero continuously as a function of temperature for γ = 0, 100 while it drops to zero abruptly for γ = 500, indicating two diﬀerent types of phase transitions.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says gamma = 0, 100 continuous, but the Fig. 2 caption says gamma = 1, 100 continuous (and its panel (c) caption lists gamma = 0, 100, 500 in the first sentence). Run count, repeats and error bars are not stated, so the first-order versus second-order identification rests on single magnetization-versus-temperature curves on a 400-spin lattice with guides to the eye. Temperature is in microwatt units.

assertions.value: The authors report that a full Monte-Carlo simulation using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (one randomly chosen spin flipped each time, accepted with the Boltzmann probability) reproduces the experimental observations, with numerical results qualitatively the same as the experimental results.
assertions.anchor: Experimental results and numerical simulations, p.3, Fig. 2(d)
quotes: These experimental observations can be reproduced with a full Monte-Carlo numerical simulation.
we randomly choose one spin each time to ﬂip in order to reduce the total energy.
the numerical results are qualitatively the same as the experimental results.

assertions.value: The authors state that one mechanism for the discrepancy between simulation and experiment is optical loss, which is not captured in their theoretical model.
assertions.anchor: Experimental results and numerical simulations, p.3
quotes: One of the mechanisms for the discrepancy is related to the optical loss, which is not captured in our theoretical model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limit of the model stated by the authors on p.3.

assertions.value: The authors report a numerical phase diagram, from scanning the four-body coefficient gamma and the effective temperature T, with a second-order phase transition for small gamma and a first-order phase transition for large positive gamma. Assuming uniform two-body and four-body constants gives a qualitatively similar phase diagram.
assertions.anchor: Experimental results and numerical simulations, p.3, Fig. 3(a,b)
quotes: The phase diagram indicates that there is a second-order phase transition for small γ and a ﬁrst-order phase transition for large positive γ.
We further assume a uniform two-body and four-body spin interaction constants and obtain a qualitatively similar phase diagram shown in Fig. 3(b).
assertions.reader_inference: The phase diagram is simulated, not measured; the paper shows no experimental phase diagram.

assertions.value: The authors develop a mean-field theory in which the two-body and four-body spin interaction constants are assumed to be uniform and the fluctuation of the spin magnetization is small.
quotes: we develop a mean-ﬁeld (MF) theory where the two-body and four-body spin interaction constants are assumed to be uniform and the ﬂuctuation of the spin magnetization is small.
assertions.certainty_reason: Assumptions of the mean-field theory stated in the Mean-field theory section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the mean-field approximation is reliable as the spin interaction in their model is long ranged.
quotes: The MF approximation is reliable as the spin interaction in our model is long ranged.
assertions.reader_inference: No argument or test of the approximation is given beyond comparison with the uniform-interaction simulation in Fig. 3(b).

assertions.value: The authors report that uniform two-body and four-body spin interactions with J ≈ 0.19µW and K ≈ 3.6×10−9µW were used in the Fig. 3(b,c) phase diagrams.
quotes: we have used uniform two-body and fourbody spin interactions with J ≈ 0.19µW , K ≈ 3.6×10−9µW .
assertions.certainty_reason: Parameters stated in the Fig. 3 caption.

assertions.value: The authors derive a self-consistent equation for the magnetization, m = tanh[(2JmN + 4γKm3N 3)/T ] (the printed m3 and N 3 are m cubed and N cubed), and state that taking the solution that minimizes the free energy yields the ground state magnetization. They report that the resulting mean-field phase diagram is consistent with the Monte-Carlo simulation with uniform interactions.
quotes: m = tanh[(2JmN + 4γKm3N 3)/T ].
Solving this equation and taking the solution that minimizes the free energy of the spin model yields the ground state magnetization.
The MF phase diagram is shown in Fig. 3(c) which is consistent with that obtained from the Monte-Carlo simulation in the presence of a uniform spin-spin interaction (Fig. 3(b)).
assertions.reader_inference: The derivation is reported as 'a straightforward calculation'; the intermediate steps are not shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that for gamma = 0 the coefficient of the quartic term in the free-energy expansion is always positive, so by Landau's theory only a second-order phase transition is possible unless odd magnetization terms appear, and that the critical temperature is Tc = 2N J (from setting the quadratic coefficient to zero).
quotes: For γ = 0, the coeﬃcient of the quartic term is always positive.
only second-order phase transition is possible unless there are odd terms of magnetization appearing in the free energy expansion
Hence, we ﬁnd Tc = 2N J.
assertions.reader_inference: Holds within the stated mean-field assumptions (uniform interactions, small fluctuations); the paper states no formal theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the second-order phase transition persists for smaller positive values of gamma because the coefficient of the quartic term remains positive at T ≈ Tc, and that the behavior changes dramatically for large enough positive gamma because the quartic coefficient changes sign.
quotes: Speciﬁcally, the second-order phase transition persists for smaller positive values of γ as the coeﬃcient of the quartic term remains positive at T ≈ Tc.
The phase transition behavior changes dramatically for large enough positive value of γ since the coeﬃcient of the quartic term changes sign.

assertions.value: The authors derive a critical value of the four-body coefficient by setting the quartic coefficient to zero at T = Tc, γc = J/(6N 2K) (the printed N 2 is N squared), and report γc ≈ 55 for the Fig. 3(c) parameters, which they state is very close to the exact numerical value. They attribute the discrepancy to ignoring higher-order terms in the expansion.
quotes: By letting it equal to zero at T = Tc, we ﬁnd a critical value of the four-body coeﬃcient γc = J/(6N 2K).
Using the parameters for Fig. 3(c), we ﬁnd γc ≈ 55 which is very close to the exact numerical value.
The discrepancy is due to the ignorance of higher-order terms in the expansion
assertions.reader_inference: The 'exact numerical value' is not given in the text; it can be read only from Fig. 3(c). The value 55 is reproduced by J = 0.19, K = 3.6e-9 and N = 400.

assertions.value: The authors state that for gamma > γc a local minimum at m = 0 appears in the free energy, and the system exhibits a first-order phase transition if this new minimum becomes a global minimum at a higher temperature. They estimate the ferromagnetic-paramagnetic boundary from F (m = 0) = F (m = 1) as γ = T (ln 2)/(KN 3) − J/(KN 2) (the printed N 3 and N 2 are N cubed and N squared), and conclude that the critical temperature for the first-order transition increases linearly with the four-body coefficient.
quotes: For γ > γc, a local minimum at m = 0 appears in the free energy and the system exhibits a ﬁrst-order phase transition if this new minimum at m = 0 becomes a global minimum at a higher temperature.
can be estimated using the condition F (m = 0) = F (m = 1), which gives the simpliﬁed form γ = T (ln 2)/(KN 3) − J/(KN 2).
Therefore, the critical temperature for the ﬁrst-order phase transition increases linearly as a function of the four-body coeﬃcient.
assertions.reader_inference: The boundary compares only m = 0 and m = 1 (full saturation); a magnetization below 1 at the transition would shift it. The paper calls the agreement with the numerical phase diagram qualitative.

assertions.value: The authors report that for gamma < 0 the system also exhibits a second-order phase transition, and that the magnetization in the ferromagnetic phase decreases as gamma changes from 0 to −500 in order to suppress the four-body spin interaction energy.
quotes: For γ < 0, our system also exhibits a second-order phase transition.
the magnetization in the ferromagnetic phase decreases as γ changes from 0 to −500 in order to suppress the fourbody spin interaction energy.

assertions.value: The authors report, from Monte-Carlo simulation and experiment for gamma < 0, a spatially structured magnetic phase: the inner part of the SLM is ferromagnetic with all spins in one direction, and the outer part shows long-range anti-ferromagnetic order with spins at opposite corners of the SLM pointing in opposite directions, separated by a domain wall.
assertions.anchor: Nonuniform spin interaction section, p.5, Fig. 4
quotes: For γ < 0, our Monte-Carlo numerical simulation and experimental observation indicate that
there is a spatially-structured magnetic phase appearing: the inner part of the SLM exhibits a ferromagnetic phase with all the spins pointing to the same direction
the outer part of the SLM exhibits a longrange anti-ferromagnetic (AF) phase with these spins located at the opposite corners of the SLM pointing to opposite directions
Consequently, a domain wall that separates the two regions of opposite spins is formed on the SLM
assertions.reader_inference: Evidence is the spin-configuration insets of Fig. 4; the text layer holds no quantitative values for them.

assertions.value: The authors report, in the last figure, zero-temperature magnetization versus negative four-body coefficient (experimental and numerical), and that the magnetization saturates to a nonzero value for large |γ|.
quotes: Zero temperature magnetic phases of the nonlinear optical Ising machine with a negative four-body coeﬃcient γ < 0.
The magnetization saturates to a nonzero value for large |γ|.

assertions.value: The authors explain the structured phase by the profile of the reduced four-body interaction matrix Qij, which has larger elements for spins at opposite sides of the SLM, so those spins favor opposite directions; in the inner part where the light intensity is stronger, the two-body interaction dominates and favors the ferromagnetic phase.
quotes: This can be understood with the proﬁle of the reduced four-body spin interaction matrix Qij (Fig. 1(c))
the spins located at the opposite side of the SLM favor opposite directions
the inner part of the SLM where the light intensity is stronger, the two-body interaction dominates
assertions.reader_inference: A qualitative explanation; no calculation is shown that separates this mechanism from alternatives.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to the best of their knowledge, their results are the first experimental observation of two types of phase transitions in a configurable optical Ising model with fully connected two-body and four-body spin interactions.
quotes: To the best of our knowledge, our results represent the ﬁrst experimental observation of two types of phase transitions in a conﬁgurable optical Ising model with fully connected two-body and four-body spin interactions.

assertions.value: The authors state that similar Ising models with nearest-neighbor two-body and local four-body spin interactions were explored theoretically in the 1970s (cited to references 42 to 44).
quotes: similar Ising models with nearest-neighbor two-body and local four-body spin interactions have been theoretically explored in the 1970s [42–44].

assertions.value: The authors pose as the natural question whether the nonlinear optical Ising machine can be used to solve optimization problems more efficiently, and describe their work only as a first step: an investigation of the ground state magnetic phases. The paper reports no optimization benchmark.
quotes: A natural question that arises is whether such a nonlinear optical Ising machine can be used to solve optimization problems more eﬃciently.
As the ﬁrst step to address this important question, we experimentally and theoretically investigate the ground state magnetic phases
assertions.reader_inference: No combinatorial optimization instance, solution quality or time-to-solution is reported anywhere in the text, so the abstract's optimization potential is not tested here.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the rich phase diagram is a direct consequence of the competition between two-body and four-body spin interactions at different effective temperature.
quotes: The exhibited rich phase diagram is a direct consequence of the competition between twobody and four-body spin interactions at diﬀerent eﬀective temperature.

assertions.value: The authors suggest that the machine may be useful for optimization problems where the four-body coefficient is gradually tuned for simulated annealing in order to quickly find the optimal solution, and that it can be generalized to antiferromagnetic or random two-body interactions and higher-order interactions through sum frequency generation, four-wave mixing and high harmonic generation. None of this is demonstrated in the paper.
quotes: may be useful for solving optimization problems where the four-body spin interaction coeﬃcient can be gradually tuned for simulated annealing in order to quickly ﬁnd the optimal solution
Our system can be further generalized by considering an antiferromagnetic or random two-body spin interactions
